SMSC
At Wilson's, we take a very proactive approach to supporting the spiritual, moral, social and cultural development of students. Through many aspects of school life we take the opportunity to promote the fundamental British values of democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty and mutual respect and tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs. This is evident in the rich PSHE programmes at all Key Stages as well as in the teaching of other subjects in the curriculum.

pageCache.pageTitle: Welcome to Wilson’s - The Sunday Times Secondary School of the Year 2024
pageCache.text:
Welcome to Wilson’s
Welcome to Wilson's School. I have been part of this truly exceptional community for over 20 years, and it has been my privilege to lead the school through such an exciting period of development since 2014.
Parents choose Wilson's not just because of the outstanding academic outcomes of students but also because they understand and share the school's values. These are encapsulated by the motto: Non Sibi Sed Omnibus (Not For Oneself, But For All). We strive to create a safe and kind environment where every pupil can become more confident and reach the highest levels of academic enjoyment and achievement. Pupils flourish at Wilson's.
Read more about the school's commitment to Inclusion and Equality here.
We are deeply proud of what we offer, particularly the hugely enriching experiences pupils enjoy beyond the classroom. Indeed these rival (and often exceed) those of fee-paying schools. Teachers engage pupils with challenging and enjoyable lessons, enriched with great activities to extend pupils’ interests and skills far beyond the National Curriculum and examination specifications. Teachers know the pupils very well and visitors often comment on the warmth and good-humour that characterise relationships between boys and members of staff.
Our expectations of pupils' personal conduct are very high, but this is matched by a unique pastoral system that teaches pupils our core values of respect, tolerance, courtesy, cooperation, service to the community, personal achievement and hard work. Please take time to watch this short video that explains more about the proactive support that we provide to pupils.
We welcome boys from a wide variety of ethnic and cultural backgrounds and we cherish the diversity and richness that this brings.
Places at the school are awarded on the basis of performance in entrance tests (which take place in the autumn term). We understand that the application process might seem daunting, but full details can be found on the Admissions section of the website and we will be happy to answer any questions you might have.
We hope you enjoy looking at our website - don't miss the latest news, which always provides a great snapshot of what has been happening in recent weeks - and we look forward to welcoming you to one of our Open Evenings, which take place in the summer term.
NJ ColeExecutive Head

pageCache.pageTitle: Sixth Form | Personal development, wellbeing and preparation for adult life
pageCache.text:
Sixth Form
Personal development, wellbeing and preparation for adult life
Sixth Form is a period of considerable personal as well as intellectual growth. At Wilson’s, wellbeing is therefore understood broadly: not simply as support when a student encounters difficulty, but as the development of the knowledge, habits, confidence and personal resources that enable young people to flourish now and sustain their wellbeing in adult life.
We recognise that aiming very high can bring pressures of its own. Students are encouraged to retain perspective, balance demanding academic ambitions with other interests and relationships, and develop healthy and sustainable ways of responding to challenge, uncertainty and occasional disappointment. Increasing independence is carefully graduated: Sixth Formers enjoy greater freedom and assume greater responsibility, while continuing to be known, guided and supported.
Through PSHE and Futures, students develop the knowledge and practical skills required for that increasing independence: managing demanding academic study, maintaining healthy relationships, understanding self-care, developing resilience, managing money, resolving conflict, communicating confidently in social and professional settings, and preparing for the practical realities of university, employment and more independent living. The published Futures programme specifically addresses A-level study skills, post-18 choices, purposeful work experience, meaningful volunteering, scholarly reading, professional communication, budgeting, living with others, independence and resilience.
Careers education, high-quality work experience and the Next Steps programme form an important part of this preparation for future wellbeing. They help students understand themselves and the world beyond school, make informed choices and approach major transitions with confidence and purpose.
Alongside this universal and preventative provision sits a strong structure of pastoral care. Academic tutors and the Sixth Form team know students well and monitor their academic progress and wider wellbeing. The Wellbeing Centre provides an accessible focus for support, while DISCOVER and the school’s wider mental-health provision offer more targeted help. The school draws readily on external professional expertise where this can provide additional or more specialist support (Wilson's School).
Leadership, service and contribution
Becoming a Sixth Former also means taking a new place within Wilson’s. Sixth formers are not simply the oldest students in the school: they are essential to its day-to-day life and effective operation, and are trusted with significant opportunities to lead, serve and influence the community around them.
Through the prefect system they serve the wider student body prominently at break and lunchtime, providing leadership, visibility and positive example, while also taking substantial responsibility across curricular and co-curricular provision. They all lead vertical tutor groups, play prominent roles within Houses and contribute extensively to sport, music, drama, CCF, societies and the school’s Charities, Equalities, Wellbeing and Environment committees. Senior prefects meet the Director of Sixth Form every fortnight, ensuring that student voice contributes meaningfully to the continuing development of Sixth Form and wider school life.
Through Civitas, every Lower Sixth student also devotes protected time to experiences beyond academic study, encompassing service to others, creativity and physical activity. Together with Wilson’s extensive co-curricular programme — including opportunities such as the Combined Cadet Force, Duke of Edinburgh’s Award, music, drama, sport, societies and debating — this gives students opportunities to try something new, pursue existing passions, contribute to others and develop confidence, resilience, teamwork, leadership and a strong sense of responsibility.
PSHE, Futures, RE and Philosophy, assemblies, tutorials, Moral Maze and the wider cultural life of the school invite students to encounter challenging ideas, engage respectfully with different perspectives, reflect upon their own values and understand their responsibilities to the communities of which they are part. The intention is to develop young adults capable not merely of academic success, but of thoughtful, informed and responsible participation in the wider world. Wilson’s published Citizenship curriculum similarly describes Key Stage 5 as developing independent thinkers with a strong sense of civic responsibility through global issues, leadership, community opportunities, critical thinking, debate and volunteering.
Exceptionally well prepared for what comes next
The Wilson’s Sixth Form is therefore much more than an academically successful programme of A-level study. These are two years in which students are expected to work hard and aim high, but also to explore, question, lead, contribute, develop new interests and grow in independence. It is a coherent preparation for higher education, employment and adult life, deliberately combining exceptional teaching and achievement with scholarship, personal development, wellbeing, independence, leadership, service and responsibility.
Students leave Wilson’s exceptionally well qualified, but that is only one measure of success. Our ambition is that they look back on Sixth Form as an intellectually exciting and personally fulfilling period of their lives, and leave with the curiosity, self-knowledge, resilience, confidence and judgement to think for themselves, embrace the opportunities and challenges ahead and, true to Non sibi sed omnibus, use their talents not only for themselves but in service to others.
For more on the Sixth Form experience and curriculum, please see here.

A great start for music
It has been a fantastic start to the new school year for the music department, with students across the school throwing themselves into rehearsals.
We have been delighted to welcome Mr Thomas Motley as our new Director of Music, joining a very experienced and talented team of teachers. Mr Motley has been getting to know students and colleagues across the department and has been hugely encouraged by the enthusiasm and commitment he has seen in rehearsals.
There has been plenty of musical activity already, with particularly strong starts for Symphony Orchestra, Odyssey Big Band and Cambiata, as well as smaller ensembles including Chamber Choir, Skiaull and Clarinet Ensemble. It has been wonderful to see so many students coming together to make music, with rehearsals already sounding very promising.
We have a number of exciting events coming up, with Chamber Choir rehearsing Stanford's Evening Service in C and Rachmaninov's Bogoroditsye Dyevo for their evensong recital at St Michael and All Angels on Tuesday, 10 November, and Big Band preparing a range of music for our first ever Rock and Jazz Night on Tuesday 8 December! The Winter Concert will take place on Wednesday, 2 December.
Congratulations to all our musicians on such an enthusiastic start. We are looking forward to an exciting year music across the school.

pageCache.pageTitle: Personal Development and Wellbeing | Wilson's School
pageCache.text:
Personal Development and Wellbeing
Personal Development and Wellbeing is at the heart of our ambition for every pupil to flourish; this is underpinned by exceptional pastoral care.
At Wilson’s, personal development and wellbeing are integral to our ambition for every pupil to flourish. Our aim is to provide a safe and kind environment in which pupils grow in confidence, develop independence and resilience, and learn to treat others with respect, tolerance and consideration. This development is deliberately planned through the curriculum as well as through the wider life of the school. Every year group receives PSHE teaching from a specialist team of teachers, with a carefully sequenced programme covering health, relationships and life in the wider world; RSE develops pupils’ understanding of healthy relationships, consent, equality, online safety and how to recognise and seek help with harmful or abusive situations. Teaching is highly inclusive. Beyond PSHE (and the Futures Programme in Years 11 and 12), our Enrichment curriculum broadens pupils’ experience further: the Year 9 Elizabethan programme develops cultural knowledge and public speaking, while later activities include practical experiences such as cookery, ICT, interview skills and preparation for work experience. Pupils learn from the experiences of a range of visiting speakers in both PSHE and the WRL programme, often including inspiring former students of the school. Together, these opportunities support pupils in becoming reflective, responsible young people who can make informed decisions and contribute positively to the communities in which they live.
Pastoral care lies at the heart of school life and is designed to ensure that pupils are known as individuals and know where to turn when they need support. In Years 7-11 every form has two tutors who monitor pupils’ wellbeing and academic progress, promote respect, responsibility and resilience, and work closely with the Head of Year, who has overall pastoral and academic responsibility for the year group. Pupil Support Managers work alongside the SENCO and safeguarding teams to coordinate individual support where required, this can include signposting to more specialist provision; Sixth Form students can also access the DISCOVER programme for anxiety, low mood and stress. The Wellbeing Centre provides a visible focus for this support, including the Benjamin Room, a counselling room and an informal space where pupils can meet and talk, and all pupils are introduced to the Centre as somewhere not just for current problems but for planning for their future wellbeing. Mental health and wellbeing are discussed through PSHE, form time and assemblies from pupils’ first week in Year 7 onwards, helping to create a culture in which seeking support is normal, understood and encouraged.
Personal development at Wilson’s also means giving pupils rich opportunities to discover interests, develop talents, serve others and prepare confidently for their next steps. Our extensive co-curricular programme encompasses sport, music, drama, chess, debating and pupil-led publications, alongside the Duke of Edinburgh’s Award and our long-established Combined Cadet Force; pupils can perform in junior and senior drama productions, join orchestras, choirs and ensembles, take part in a wide range of competitive and recreational sports, or challenge themselves through expeditions and leadership opportunities. This breadth is complemented by a structured careers programme: pupils encounter careers and the world of work through lessons, assemblies, visiting speakers and external events; all pupils have the opportunity for an individual careers interview, with Year 11 and Year 12 students receiving one as part of their programme, and Sixth Form provision includes a Higher Education Fair, university and apprenticeship guidance, personal-statement support and extensive interview preparation. In this way, the school’s motto, Non Sibi Sed Omnibus — not for oneself, but for all — is lived through opportunities that build character, cooperation, aspiration and service, helping pupils to leave Wilson’s exceptionally well prepared for higher education, employment and fulfilling adult lives.
Enrichment
At Wilson’s, Personal Development and Wellbeing extends far beyond the PSHE and Citizenship curriculum and Work Related Learning programme. Our Enrichment Curriculum is a universal offer - enjoyed by all - and central to the Wilson's experience. This is then complemented by an extensive range of wider opportunities - clubs, societies and competitions - through which pupils discover new interests and develop their talents. In keeping with our Aims and Ethos, this provision is broad, purposeful and carefully planned.
The enrichment curriculum includes a wide range of taught experiences such as (to illustrate) cookery; the Year 7 Music Programme; Games and Sport and distinctive programmes including The Elizabethan, Year 10 Enrichment and Futures ( extending into Year 12). All pupils also benefit from a wide range of trips and visits. Together, these ensure that enrichment is woven through pupils’ wider experience of school life rather than confined to individual lessons.
Alongside this universal provision sits an exceptional breadth of co-curricular activity. Over a hundred clubs and activities give pupils opportunities both to pursue existing interests and to try something new. These encompass Music, sport, drama and performance, debating and public speaking, chess, academic societies and publications, creative activities, leadership and service, the Combined Cadet Force and the Duke of Edinburgh’s Award.
Our enrichment provision is reviewed regularly and - although it long predates their existence - reflects the ambition of the Department for Education’s Enrichment Benchmarks. Every pupil benefits from the breadth of the Personal Development offer at Wilson’s: our Latest News gives a flavour of the range of activities, events and achievements taking place across the school each week.

Wilson’s students reading together
As part of our Wilson’s Reading Together strategy, pupils across the school have been enjoying a new short story each week to read along with a recording, with staff joining in too. This term's first story, Where There Is Water There Is Life by Joanna Davidson is part of a collection of short stories called War Stories, curated by former Children's Laureate, Michael Morpurgo.
2026 is the National Year of Reading, a UK-wide campaign encouraging people of all ages to rediscover the enjoyment of reading. The campaign highlights the importance of making reading part of everyday life, rather than seeing it simply as a school task.
By creating a regular opportunity for everyone to read together, Wilson’s Reading Together aims to give students the chance to discover new stories, enjoy reading for its own sake and share that experience as a school community.
We look forward to discovering where the next story takes us!

Hands-on biology in Dissection Club
This lunchtime club brings together pupils from Years 9 to 11, with our Year 13 Biology students helping to lead practical sessions and share their enthusiasm for the subject. The first session got off to an exciting start with a heart dissection, giving students the opportunity to explore the structure and function of the heart first-hand.
There is plenty more to look forward to this term, with upcoming dissections including kidneys, eyes, locusts and chicken wings.
A big thank you to our Year 13 Biologists for helping to lead the sessions and to everyone who came along for such an enthusiastic start. We are looking forward to seeing the club continue to grow throughout the term.

pageCache.pageTitle: A great start for the Class of 2033!
pageCache.text:
A great start for the Class of 2033!
School life is now well underway for our new Year 7 pupils, whose first few days at Wilson’s were devoted to induction activities designed to help them settle quickly and confidently into their new surroundings.
These included a Treasure Trail around the school, activities with their tutor groups and exciting activities organised by the Music and Sports departments. Pupils also benefited from practical guidance on some of the routines of everyday school life, such as using their cubby holes, valuables lockers and homework diaries.
Alongside these preparations, our new pupils have been reminded of the fundamental importance of kindness, consideration and politeness. In particular, they have been encouraged to look out for anyone who may be finding the transition to secondary school difficult. Every pupil has a part to play in ensuring that those around them feel welcomed, valued and included.
We look forward to getting to know our new pupils — and their parents — better over the months ahead, including at the New Year 7 Parents’ Social Evening.
Pictures of our new Year 7s settling into life at Wilson’s will soon be available on the school’s Instagram account, alongside other recent news from the school.
We wish all Wilson’s pupils, staff and parents a successful and fulfilling year ahead!

pageCache.pageTitle: A winning streak for Wilson's athletes
pageCache.text:
A winning streak for Wilson's athletes
It has been a fantastic few weeks for the Wilson’s Athletics Teams. Earlier this month the Junior Boys Team, comprising of students from Years 7 and 8, travelled down to Kent to compete in the English Schools’ Regional Final. Some fantastic performances, in particular from Logan (Year 7), who equalled the school record in the 1500m and Woody (Year 8) with a dominant run in the 300m, saw Wilson’s place above local rivals John Fisher, Wallington Boys and only one place behind Whitgift. An excellent effort all round.
Moving onto Borough Sports on 26 June, the weather was hot and the boys were on fire! Our students performed exceptionally well across each year group, achieving:
These outstanding performances meant that we finished 1st overall, winning the competition by an impressive 26 points with John Fisher in 2nd and Wallington Boys in 3rd. This is a tremendous achievement and reflects the hard work, commitment, and determination of all the students involved.
A special mention to two students, Max (Year 9) and James (Year 10), who are also Surrey Schools’ Champions, winning gold medals in the Triple Jump and 100m Hurdles. A big congratulations to them both.
We look forward to Sports Day and the exciting times that lay ahead for Wilson’s athletics.

Music Programme
Wilsons's School is a leading boys’ state grammar school, offering a free education to nearly 1,300 pupils aged 11-18. The Wilson’s School Music Programme seeks applications into Year 7 for boys showing an aptitude for music. Wilson’s outstanding academic record is matched by its dedication to music and the arts.
There are up to 9 priority places to offer pupils displaying potential for music.
Music at Wilson'sThe Music Department at Wilson’s is exceptional and has been described as one of the very best in the UK. Teaching in the department is outstanding and delivered by very highly-qualified teachers; there is a very rich co-curricular programme for pupils of all abilities.
Academic MusicLessons are practical and creative at all key stages and pupils are taught in small classes. Examination results at GCSE and A level are very strong (100% A* at A level in both 2020 and 2022), and a considerable number of students have continued to study music at university beyond Wilson’s over recent years, including at Oxford and Cambridge, as well as other excellent universities and music colleges.
Co-curricular MusicPupils at Wilson’s are able to join a large range of ensembles to match their experience and enthusiasm, with senior students playing more challenging repertoire in the Senior Orchestra, String Orchestra and Chamber Wind Ensembles. Over 100 boys sing in the school choir. During a normal school year, we host well over thirty-five concerts, recitals, productions and other musical events.
The Year 7 ProgrammeNearly a decade ago, the department began to offer free specialist tuition in voice or a musical instrument to every pupil in Year 7. All pupils start a new instrument as part of the programme and the instruments and equipment are provided free of charge to pupils. Many students continue to play their instruments beyond Year 7 and they prove to be enthusiastic and accomplished members of our various ensembles. Pupils who have started learning in Year 7 have obtained places at music colleges as well as Oxbridge choral scholarships.
Britton CentreIn January 2023, the Britton Centre, the new home of the Music Department was opened, and the building has been buzzing with musical activity ever since. The Britton Centre houses a recital hall, home to two grand pianos and a battery of professional percussion instruments, a recording studio, three large classrooms, each equipped with computers for composition, a piano and a drumkit, and many new practice rooms, all professionally sound-proofed.
Wilson’s provides an outstanding all-round education for free. We are a selective grammar school for academically able boys.
Parents regularly tell us that they choose Wilson’s not just for our excellent academic record but because of the broad spectrum of extra-curricular activities we offer. These include many sports clubs, a thriving Combined Cadet Force section, an established Duke of Edinburgh’s Award scheme and a unique music programme that allows every Year 7 pupil to learn a musical instrument as part of the curriculum.
How this is achieved…
Our expectations of boys in terms of personal achievement – academic and otherwise – and behaviour are very high. We have an excellent pastoral system that communicates our core values of respect, tolerance, courtesy, cooperation, service to the community, personal achievement and most of all, hard work. Our school motto – Non Sibi Sed Omnibus (Not For Oneself, But For All) – drives all that we do. In 2015 we opened our Lower School providing a nurturing and supportive environment to help our Year 7 pupils make the challenging transition from primary to secondary school. Most of their lessons are taught in their form room which provides them with the security of their own classroom and the familiarity of surroundings they are used to at primary school.
Our outstanding all-round provision has been recognised in our being awarded the Sunday Times State Secondary School of the Year in 2019, a Sunday Times Top 10 State Secondary School in 2020 and the Sunday Times London State Secondary School of the Decade in 2021. In September 2022, Ofsted rated the school Outstanding.
Wilson’s prides itself on the fact that this is achieved whilst being a state-funded school. This means the education and wider opportunities we provide are free: no fees are payable for any pupil who gains a place at the school.
Music Programme Entry Requirements
Pupils gaining a place under the Wilson’s School Music Programme scheme are expected to commit to school ensembles throughout their time at the school.
Please see our Year 7 admissions criteria here for full details about admissions into Wilson’s School.
Wilson’s is a selective grammar school, selecting on the basis of academic ability. Up to 9 boys, having passed the two-stage entrance test, will be eligible for priority places based upon their aptitude for music.
Music Aptitude places are awarded to candidates by:
Therefore, of all applicants passing the school’s two-stage entrance test, places will be awarded in this order:
If your son participates in the Music Aptitude Test but is not successful in meeting the required threshold to be considered for one of these places, he can still be considered for a place at the school under the other admission criteria provided he has passed the entrance examinations. Taking part in the Music Aptitude Test in no way disadvantages your son in his chances of gaining a place in the school under other of the admission criteria. On the day of the Music Aptitude Test, candidates will be tested on various aspects of their musicianship potential through both listening and practical activities.
Please note that no part of the Music Aptitude Test requires any familiarity with music theory or other previous musical knowledge.
One element that candidates will need to prepare in advance is a solo performance. Candidates will need to prepare a short performance on their preferred instrument or voice. Candidates will then work with an assessor, responding to their instructions and suggestions, to develop their singing or playing of their piece.
For more information about the Music Aptitude Test process please see the Aptitude Places Process page of this website.
The Music Aptitude Test will take place on Saturday 10 October 2026. If you want your son to be considered for a music aptitude place all you need to do is register your son to sit the Selective Eligibility Test (SET) which you can do via the school’s website. If he passes the SET for Wilson’s School you will be given instructions on how to register your son to participate in the Music Aptitude test.

Reading
At Wilson’s, reading is regarded as central to academic excellence, intellectual curiosity and personal development. Pupils arrive as strong, committed readers, and the school builds on this foundation through a carefully planned approach.
A structured and long-standing programme spanning Years 7 to 13 fosters a strong culture of reading. In Key Stage 3, the English Department delivers a curated reading programme, monitored by class teachers, which ensures that all pupils engage regularly with a broad range of high-quality texts. This establishes strong habits of reading and discussion early in pupils’ time at the school and extends beyond the curriculum itself.
At Key Stage 4, reading is further developed through the Elizabethan Reading Programme, which offers pupils access to a wide range of texts beyond the examined curriculum and encourages continued reading for both interest and enrichment.
At Key Stage 5, a rich super-curricular offer, curated by individual departments, supports pupils in developing sophisticated disciplinary knowledge through reading, preparing them for higher education and future ambitions.
Across the school, pupils are supported to engage critically with a range of texts and sources, including through opportunities within the Global Politics enrichment curriculum, where they develop research and referencing skills and engage with contemporary issues.
Building Strong Reading Habits
Developing strong readers is rooted in consistent, well-established habits. At Key Stage 3, all pupils have a reading book, enabling regular reading during form time. This sits within a carefully designed reading programme, overseen by the English Department, which ensures that pupils are exposed to a broad range of high-quality and appropriately challenging texts. Reading habits are reinforced by form tutors, English teachers and the Librarian, who guide pupils in their choices.
Wilson’s Reading Together
Wilson’s Reading Together is a whole-school initiative that promotes reading as a shared, everyday habit. Each week, pupils engage with a short story during tutor time.
Texts are carefully selected to expose pupils to a wide range of themes, perspectives and styles. Recordings by staff from across the school model reading for pleasure and reinforce the importance of reading within the Wilson’s community.
Access to High-Quality Reading
The Library sits at the centre of reading at Wilson’s, offering a wide range of fiction, non-fiction and academic texts. Supported by the Librarian, pupils are guided towards ambitious and engaging reading, while the space itself provides a calm environment for independent study and reflection.
All pupils have access to Sora, providing e-books, audiobooks and The Week. In addition, The Day supports engagement with current affairs. These resources strengthen media literacy and support pupils in evaluating information critically.
Reading as Enrichment
The Elizabethan Programme provides pupils with access to a curated range of influential texts beyond the core curriculum. These works introduce key ideas across disciplines, encouraging discussion, critical thinking and intellectual curiosity.
Reading Across the Curriculum
Reading is embedded across all subjects and underpins disciplinary understanding.
Across the curriculum, pupils are expected to read critically, assess reliability and form evidence-based conclusions.

Wellbeing Mentors at Wilson's
At Wilson’s, we want every student to know that they do not have to face challenges alone. Our specially trained Year 13 peer mentors play an important role in creating a supportive and compassionate school community. Around 25 students take part in the programme, completing two half-day training sessions with the Education Wellbeing Service to prepare them for their role. As positive role models, they offer something particularly valuable: the guidance of an older student who already has some experience of the challenges their younger peers may be facing.
The impact of this thoughtful, low-key approach to support was recognised at the Mental Health Conference in June, where this good practice was shared. The delegates responded enthusiastically to both the programme and the students who presented it, celebrating the important contribution peer mentors make to student wellbeing.
Egemen (Year 13) shares his perspective on this, below.
The Wellbeing Team at Wilson's works to foster an environment of comfort and compassion where every student feels able to reach out and seek support when needed. We aim to make this process as easy as possible by providing many routes to wellbeing support.
There are many ways to access support, including our specially trained Year 13 peer mentor team who facilitate one-on-one peer mentor sessions, where students can openly talk about anything weighing on their mind, whether big, small or simply a difficult day. Our peer mentors offer a calm, confidential space and build trust by regularly meeting up with their mentees in the school's dedicated Wellbeing Centre.
Our peer mentors are also around the Wellbeing Centre during lunchtimes, so if you see them, please come and say hello. You do not need to have a particular problem or know exactly what you want to talk about; sometimes, the first step is simply starting a conversation.

Year 11 celebrate outstanding GCSE results
Congratulations to our Year 11 pupils, who are celebrating a record-breaking set of GCSE results.
An extraordinary 66% of GCSEs at Wilson’s were awarded Grade 9, the highest grade available in the GCSE system. The performance of our pupils places the school among the very highest-achieving schools in the country.
Of the 1,965 GCSE qualifications awarded, 1,305 received a Grade 9, while 96.2% of all grades were at Grades 9–7.
These exceptional results are a tremendous achievement. Congratulations once again to all of our pupils and staff for the hard work, commitment and dedication that made them possible.

SEN & Disabilities
Wilson’s School is committed to ensuring that pupils with special educational needs and or disabilities (SEND) flourish in every aspect of school life. We maintain high expectations for every pupil while recognising that some will need reasonable adjustments, adaptations or additional support to overcome barriers to their learning or wellbeing.
Our provision follows the graduated Assess → Plan → Do → Review approach. Needs are identified early through assessment, classroom observation, information from teachers and pastoral staff, and the views of pupils and their parents. Support is planned around clearly understood individual needs and reviewed regularly to evaluate its impact.
The starting point is high-quality inclusive teaching, with appropriate challenge and adaptation in every classroom. Pupil Passports and individual learning plans give staff clear, practical information about how to meet individual needs and reduce barriers. Staff receive appropriate information, training and support, and specialist advice is sought where necessary. Provision is coordinated by the SENCo and Assistant SENCo, working closely with teachers, form tutors, Heads of Year, Pupil Support Managers and senior leaders. Pupils may receive support from the school counsellor, school nurse, educational psychologist or other specialist services where appropriate. Pupils and parents are involved in planning and reviewing support. Progress and wellbeing are monitored carefully, and provision is adjusted where it is not having sufficient impact. Careful planning also supports successful transitions into Wilson’s, between stages of education and into higher education, training or employment. The kinds of special educational needs for which provision is made at the school There are four broad categories of need described in the SEND Code of Practice (2015) and Wilson’s is able to make provision for each of these:
Information and Guidance: Points of Contact Trust Board and SEN Trustee: The Trust Board is responsible for ensuring high quality policy and provision for pupils with Special Educational Needs. The SEN Trustee meets the SENCo regularly to support the evaluation of SEN provision in the school. Executive Head and Senior Leadership Team: Responsibility for monitoring and evaluating the progress of all pupils and for making strategic decisions which will maximise their opportunity to learn lies with the Head and the Senior Leadership Team. The SENCo is a member of the Associate Leadership Team. He also regularly meets with the Deputy Head (Inclusion) to ensure that SEND matters are discussed regularly at the highest levels. SENCo: The school’s SENCo has overall responsibility for pupils with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (as defined in the 2015 SEN Code of Practice), including identification and coordination of provision. The SENCo liaises with, advises and manages training for teaching staff relating to pupils with SEND and their needs, ensuring that individual plans written for pupils are put into practice. The SENCo is responsible for annual reviews and other key meetings about pupils with SEN. The SENCo manages the referral procedures to the Local Authority to request High Needs funding and/or an Education Health and Care Plan (EHC Plan) when it is suspected that a pupil may have SEND which will require significant support. The SENCo is responsible for the evaluation of the impact and effectiveness of all additional interventions for pupils with SEND and accountable as a senior leader to the Executive Head. The SENCo is responsible for liaising with other agencies and professions when necessary to support a pupil with SEND. Pupil Support Managers and Heads of Year: At Wilson’s the relevant Head of Year is normally the first point of contact for a parent wishing to discuss any concerns relating to their son. They have overall responsibility for monitoring the academic progress and wellbeing of pupils. The relevant Pupil Support Manager will also help co-ordinate the support for pupils with SEND. They liaise closely with teachers and other staff (including the SENCo) about any interventions that may be required. Class teachers: the role of the class teacher is to monitor the progress of each pupil and liaise proactively with the Pupil Support Manager, Head of Year and/or SENCo about the additional needs of particular pupils. Lesson planning by classroom teachers must take account of the individual needs of pupils with SEND and demonstrate high expectations. Designated Safeguarding Lead: The DSL is a vital point of contact whenever there is any concern about the welfare of a child. Concerns or Complaints: any parent or carer who has a concern or complaint about the support that is provided for their child with SEN should first seek to resolve the issue directly with the SENCo. However, if this does not resolve the situation then the complaint can be submitted using the school’s Complaints Procedure. Arrangements for admission of disabled pupils

The 1615 Club
Inspired by the year Wilson's School was founded, The 1615 Club is our new alumni regular giving programme which encourages Old Wilsonians to support the school on a recurring monthly basis.
To join The 1615 Club, participants must simply commit to donating £16.15 or more per calendar month through our new, easy to use two-click JustGiving portal.
Why It Matters
All money raised through The 1615 Club directly supports the maintenance and growth of our fantastic co-curricular offering at Wilson's.
Generations of alumni have enjoyed CCF, Chess, Drama, Football, Rugby, Music, Badminton, Debating, Table Tennis, Duke of Edinburgh, school trips, and much more at Mollison Drive.
Members of The 1615 Club are directly supporting the opportunities they themselves enjoyed during their school careers, and also ensuring all current students – regardless of their family’s own financial situation – are still able to access all co-curricular opportunities at Wilson’s free of charge.

Every member of The 1615 Club will receive invitations to alumni events, key news from the school, and development updates.

These events offer the opportunity to reconnect with fellow Old Wilsonians, network with attendees in a similar field, and stay closely connected with the school, hearing of its upcoming plans and recent progress.
Members of The 1615 Circle will also have access to an additional, exclusive event organised by the development office.
